paper.title: An L3 bound for the dyadic triangular Hilbert form
paper.html:
Abstract

We prove a uniform L3×L3×L3 estimate for the dyadic triangular Hilbert form with unrestricted real inputs. The sum of the absolute local contributions over any finite set of scales is bounded by forty times the product of the input norms. In particular, the bound allows coefficients of modulus at most one to vary independently among admissible interval triples.

1 Introduction

The triangular Hilbert form couples three functions of two variables, each pair sharing one variable. We study its dyadic model, in which the intervals are constrained by binary addition without carries. The estimate below imposes no structural condition on any of the three inputs.
Write R+​=[0,∞). For k∈Z, let
Dk​={[2kn,2k(n+1)):n∈Z≥0​}.
For I∈Dk​, denote its index by nI​ and set
hI​=1Ileft​​−1Iright​​.
Let ⊕ denote bitwise XOR of nonnegative integers, and define the set of admissible triples
Ak​={(I0​,I1​,I2​)∈Dk3​:nI0​​⊕nI1​​⊕nI2​​=0}.
For I∈Ak​ and three real functions Fv​ on R+2​, put
LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)=2−k∫I0​×I1​×I2​​F0​(x0​,x1​)F1​(x1​,x2​)F2​(x2​,x0​)v=0∏2​hIv​​(xv​)dx0​dx1​dx2​.(1.1)
The dyadic triangular Hilbert form with a finite set of scales S⊂Z and real coefficients ∣ϵk​∣≤1 is
ΛS,ϵd​(F0​,F1​,F2​)=k∈S∑​ϵk​I∈Ak​∑​LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​).(1.2)
Theorem 1.1.
For every finite S⊂Z and all real bounded compactly supported measurable functions F0​,F1​,F2​ on R+2​,
k∈S∑​I∈Ak​∑​∣LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)∣≤40v=0∏2​∥Fv​∥L3(R+2​)​.(1.3)
In particular, (1.2) satisfies the same product bound, uniformly in the scales and coefficients. The absolute values in (1.3) also allow a separate coefficient of modulus at most one for each admissible triple. The estimate extends to all real L3 inputs by density, as explained in Section 5.

1.1 Context and relation to earlier work

The continuous triangular Hilbert form has the same cyclic arrangement of inputs as (1.1), integrated over R3 against the principal-value kernel 1/(x0​+x1​+x2​). Its symmetric L3 estimate is formulated by Thiele in [3, Section~9, Problem~13]. That contribution also displays the precise dyadic model (1.2), with one coefficient for each scale, and asks for the analogous bound. Theorem 1.1 answers this dyadic question affirmatively and gives the stronger sum of absolute local contributions. The continuous form and its dyadic model are distinct operators; the theorem here is a statement about the latter.
Kovač, Thiele and Zorin-Kranich introduced a dyadic triangular model with coefficients allowed to vary among interval triples [6, Equations~(1.5)--(1.6)]. Their Theorem 1.7 gives uniform estimates when one input has either a specified dependence on a Walsh linear combination of its coordinates or a specified fiberwise character structure. Those cases already encompass dyadic versions of Carleson's operator and uniform bounds for the bilinear Hilbert transform, as explained in their Appendix A. Our estimate allows all three inputs to vary freely. The cyclic operator-trace representation used below also appears in their Equation (1.5).
Another line of work measures cancellation through the growth of truncated norms. Tao obtained sublogarithmic growth for one-dimensional multilinear Hilbert transforms [9, Theorem~1.2]; Zorin-Kranich proved the corresponding sublinear growth in the number of smooth scales for simplex Hilbert transforms [10, Theorem~1.3]. Durcik, Kovač and Thiele then obtained power-type cancellation in both the continuous and dyadic settings [2, Theorems~1 and~4]. For the triangular dyadic form, their bound over m consecutive scales has a factor m1/2 at exponents (4,4,2); cyclic permutation and multilinear interpolation give the same growth at (3,3,3). Theorem 1.1 removes this scale dependence at the symmetric tuple.
The strategy of controlling an entangled form by the change of a nonnegative energy has precedents in Kovač's Bellman-function framework [4, Section~2] and his telescoping identity for the twisted paraproduct [5, Lemma~2]. These provide a methodological precedent, rather than a bound for the present triangular form. In particular, Kovač explicitly identifies the obstruction to applying that framework to non-bipartite graphs, including the triangle, in [4, Section~6.2]. Here the energy is a trace of a matrix power, and the averaging is over the four children selected by the XOR constraint.
The matrix energy and the dimension-independent trace inequality are taken from the companion manuscript [7, Sections~2--3, Lemmas~2.1, 2.2 and~3.1]; we reproduce their real finite-dimensional proofs. Their underlying matrix calculus is classical: the square-root derivative is a special case of the divided-difference formula in [1, Section~1, Equation~(1)], and the order comparison uses monotonicity of the positive square root [8, Theorem, p.~309].

1.2 The energy argument

The proof reduces the form to finite matrices by taking inputs constant on sufficiently small dyadic squares. On a fixed admissible triple, each input becomes a matrix between the atom spaces of its two variables. At each variable, we join its two incident matrices into a single row operator R and assign it the energy tr((R∗R)3/2). Let e(I) be the sum of these three energies, and let ch(I) consist of the four admissible triples obtained by halving each interval. The key estimate is
∣LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)∣≤C0​22k​41​I′∈ch(I)∑​e(I′)−e(I)​,I∈Ak​,(1.4)
with an absolute constant C0​. At each scale, the weighted total energy ∑I∈Ak​​22ke(I) is bounded by an absolute constant times the sum of the cubed input norms.
To prove (1.4), a matrix trace estimate bounds the triangular product by three Hessian quadratic forms of P↦tr(P3/2). Conditional on one child half, each neighboring half remains equally likely to be left or right. The two neighbors are correlated, but RR∗ is a sum of the two edge Gram matrices; it contains no product between their multipliers and has the same nonzero spectrum as R∗R. Convexity therefore converts the Hessian bound into an increase of the child energy. Writing the local integrals in normalized interval measures leaves the weight 22k. Each child has one parent and weight 22(k−1), one quarter of the parent's weight, so these increases telescope.
Section 2 establishes the energy inequalities, Section 3 proves the trace estimate, Section 4 supplies the conditional-averaging argument, and Section 5 sums the resulting differences and passes to measurable inputs.

2 The matrix energy and its curvature

We first record the finite-dimensional facts that will measure the energy increase under a dyadic split. All spaces and matrices in the proof are real; R∗ denotes the transpose of R. For a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix P, define
Φ(P)=tr(P3/2),suppP=(kerP)⊥.
A symmetric matrix K is supported on P if it annihilates kerP. Symmetry then also puts its range in suppP. For such K, define
bP​(K)=23​i,j∑​pi​​+pj​​∣Kij​∣2​,(2.1)
where pi​>0 are the eigenvalues of P on its support, and the entries are taken in an orthonormal eigenbasis of that support. If P=0, the only supported K is zero and b0​(0)=0. Simultaneous orthogonal conjugation and extension by zero preserve Φ and b.
The next two lemmas are the real-matrix versions of the energy derivative and order comparison results in the companion manuscript [7, Section~2]. We give the proofs, including the support conventions needed for singular Gram matrices.
Lemma 2.1 (Hessian of the energy).
On matrices positive definite on a fixed support, Φ is smooth and, for a symmetric direction K on that support,
dΦP​(K)=23​tr(P​K),d2ΦP​(K,K)=bP​(K).
In particular, Φ is convex on the positive semidefinite cone.
Proof.
Work on the support and set B=P​. The derivative of the squaring map at B is
LB​(X)=BX+XB.
This is the square-root instance of the classical matrix derivative calculus [1, Section~1, Equation~(1)]. In an eigenbasis of P, this map multiplies entry (i,j) by pi​​+pj​​>0. The inverse function theorem therefore gives a smooth square root whose derivative X in direction K satisfies BX+XB=K. Differentiating tr(B3) and using cyclicity,
dΦP​(K)=3tr(B2X)=23​tr(BK).
A second differentiation gives
d2ΦP​(K,K)=23​⟨K,LB−1​K⟩HS​=bP​(K),
where ⟨X,Y⟩HS​=tr(X∗Y). The Hessian is nonnegative. This proves convexity on positive definite matrices; replacing each matrix by itself plus ηId and letting η↓0 proves convexity on the closed cone.
∎
Lemma 2.2 (Order comparison).
Suppose P,Q are positive semidefinite matrices on the same space, a≥1, and P≤aQ. Every symmetric K supported on P is supported on Q, and
bP​(K)≥a−1/2bQ​(K).(2.2)
Proof.
For x∈kerQ, the inequalities 0≤⟨Px,x⟩≤a⟨Qx,x⟩=0 imply Px=0. Thus kerQ⊆kerP, which proves the support assertion.
First suppose P,Q are positive definite. Inversion reverses positive definite order: conjugating 0<X≤Y by X−1/2, inverting the resulting matrix at least Id, and conjugating back gives Y−1≤X−1. The spectral integral
X​=π1​∫0∞​X(X+tId)−1t​dt​
then proves monotonicity of the positive square root [8, Theorem, p.~309], since X(X+tId)−1=Id−t(X+tId)−1. Consequently P​≤a​Q​.
For a positive semidefinite matrix A, left and right multiplication by A are positive semidefinite self-adjoint operators on the full Hilbert–Schmidt matrix space: their quadratic forms are tr(X∗AX) and tr(X∗XA). Hence
LP​​≤a​LQ​​,LP​−1​≥a−1/2LQ​−1​.
Taking the quadratic form at K and using Lemma 2.1 proves (2.2).
In the semidefinite case, a≥1 gives P+ηId≤a(Q+ηId). Apply the positive definite result and let η↓0. In a full eigenbasis of either matrix, every entry of K meeting its kernel is zero. Formula (2.1) therefore gives convergence to the two supported quadratic forms in (2.2).
∎
Corollary 2.3 (A midpoint gap).
If T≥0 and U=U∗ satisfy −T≤U≤T, then U is supported on T and
2Φ(T+U)+Φ(T−U)​−Φ(T)≥22​1​bT​(U).(2.3)

∎

3 A triangular trace estimate

We now compare a cyclic product of three matrices with the Hessian costs from Section 2. This is the finite-dimensional estimate that will control a local triangular integral. Its proof follows the mixed trace argument in [7, Section~3]; working over the reals lets us identify the two orientations of the triangle directly by transposition.
Let Hv​, v∈Z/3Z, be finite-dimensional real inner product spaces, and let Wv​:Hv+1​→Hv​. The two edges incident to vertex v form the row star
Rv​=[Wv​Wv−1∗​]:Hv+1​⊕Hv−1​⟶Hv​,Tv​=Rv∗​Rv​.(3.1)
The two Gram matrices Rv∗​Rv​ and Rv​Rv∗​ have the same nonzero eigenvalues with multiplicities, so their Φ values agree.
Proposition 3.1 (Mixed trace estimate).
For the maps in (3.1), let Dv​:Hv​→Hv​ be symmetric with ∥Dv​∥op​≤1, and put Uv​=Rv∗​Dv​Rv​. Then Uv​ is supported on Tv​, and

4 Energy increase under a dyadic split

We apply the matrix estimate to a fixed admissible triple and compare its energy with the average energy of its children. For this section, the inputs are bounded, compactly supported, and constant on products of intervals in Dm​, for some m∈Z.

4.1 Matrices for a local integral

For I=(I0​,I1​,I2​)∈Ak​, k≥m, let Hv​ have an orthonormal basis indexed by the intervals of Dm​ inside Iv​. Call these intervals atoms. In the probability measure ∣Iv​∣−1dxv​, each atom has weight wv​(i)=2m−k. Define Wv​:Hv+1​→Hv​ by
Wv​(i,j)=wv​(i)wv+1​(j)​Fv​(i,j),(4.1)
where Fv​(i,j) is the constant value on the corresponding atom pair. Use these maps in (3.1), and define
ev​(I)=Φ(Tv​)=Φ(Rv​Rv∗​),e(I)=v=0∑2​ev​(I).(4.2)
If k≥m+1, let Dv​ be the diagonal matrix of the hIv​​-values on the atoms, and put
τ(I)=tr(D0​W0​D1​W1​D2​W2​).
The diagonal matrices are symmetric contractions. In the expanded trace, each vertex weight occurs as two square roots, so τ(I) is exactly the normalized integral of the product of the three inputs and three Haar signs. Therefore
LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)=22kτ(I).(4.3)

4.2 The four children

If bv​∈{0,1} chooses the left or right half of Iv​, the child index is 2nIv​​+bv​. The child triple is admissible precisely when b0​⊕b1​⊕b2​=0. Equivalently, with sv​=(−1)bv​, its signs satisfy s0​s1​s2​=1. Write ch(I) for these four children. Under uniform choice among them, each sign is uniform and every pair of signs is independent. For I∈Ak​, k≥m+1, define

∣τ(I)∣≤3102​​δ(I).(4.4)
Proof.
We keep the parent spaces fixed and extend each child matrix by zero. Set

5 Summation and passage to measurable inputs

The local increase from Proposition 4.1 has the sign needed for telescoping toward finer scales. This use of an energy difference parallels the Bellman-function summations in [4, Section~2] and [5, Lemma~2]. We bound the total energy at each level before carrying out that sum.
Lemma 5.1 (Total energy).
For the step functions of Section 4 and every k≥m, set
Jk​=I∈Ak​∑​22ke(I).
Then
0≤Jk​≤22​v=0∑2​∥Fv​∥33​.(5.1)
For k≥m+1,
I∈Ak​∑​22kδ(I)=Jk−1​−Jk​.(5.2)
Proof.
If a,b are the Hilbert–Schmidt norms of the two edges incident to v, then
ev​(I)=tr(Tv3/2​)≤(trTv​)3/2=(a2+b2)3/2≤2​(a3+b3).
For an edge Wv​, its probability normalization gives
∥Wv​∥HS3​=(∣Iv​∣∣Iv+1​∣1​∫Iv​×Iv+1​​∣Fv​∣2)3/2≤∣Iv​∣∣Iv+1​∣1​∫Iv​×Iv+1​​∣Fv​∣3.(5.3)
Every edge occurs in two row stars. Also, every ordered pair of intervals in Dk​ determines exactly one admissible third interval, by XOR. Multiplication by 22k=∣Iv​∣∣Iv+1​∣ and summation of (5.3) therefore prove (5.1). These sums are finite: compact support leaves finitely many nonzero edge matrices, each belonging to one admissible triple.
Deleting the last bit of each child index shows that every admissible child has a unique admissible parent. As 22k/4=22(k−1), the child part in the definition of δ sums to Jk−1​, proving (5.2).
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.1 for step functions.
The case S=∅ is immediate. Otherwise set k−​=minS, k+​=maxS, and refine the common atom level, if necessary, so that m≤k−​−1. By (4.3), Proposition 4.1, and Lemma 5.1,
k∈S∑​I∈Ak​∑​∣LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)∣​≤3102​​k=k−​∑k+​​(Jk−1​−Jk​)≤3102​​Jk−​−1​≤340​v=0∑2​∥Fv​∥33​.​
The insertion of missing scales is valid because each energy difference is nonnegative. If every input has nonzero norm, apply this estimate to Fv​/∥Fv​∥3​. Trilinearity of each local integral gives (1.3), with constant 40. If any norm is zero, the local integrals vanish.
∎
To pass to general inputs we need continuity of the absolute sum, not merely continuity of the signed form. The following fixed-level estimate provides it.
Lemma 5.2 (Continuity at one scale).
For every k∈Z and real Fv​∈L3(R+2​),
I∈Ak​∑​∣LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)∣≤v=0∏2​∥Fv​∥3​.(5.4)
Consequently the sequence (LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​))I∈Ak​​ depends continuously on the inputs as a map from L3×L3×L3 to ℓ1(Ak​).
Proof.
Define the nonnegative edge averages
av​(I)=∣Iv​∣∣Iv+1​∣1​∫Iv​×Iv+1​​∣Fv​∣3.
Hölder's inequality on the product probability space of the three intervals, with the Haar signs bounded by one, gives
∣LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​)∣≤22kv=0∏2​av​(I)1/3.
Apply Hölder again, now to the sum over Ak​ with weight 22k. The uniqueness of the third interval yields
I∈Ak​∑​22kav​(I)=∥Fv​∥33​,
proving (5.4). These bounds also justify all integrals and absolute sums for L3 inputs.
For two input triples F,G, expand the difference of local integrals into the three terms with inputs
(F0​−G0​,F1​,F2​),(G0​,F1​−G1​,F2​),(G0​,G1​,F2​−G2​).
Estimate each term by (5.4). If Gv​→Fv​ in L3, the sum of these three product bounds tends to zero. This is the asserted ℓ1 continuity.
∎
Completion of Theorem 1.1.
Bounded compactly supported dyadic step functions are dense in L3(R+2​). To see this, first approximate an L3 function by a continuous compactly supported function, then take its averages on sufficiently small dyadic squares. Uniform continuity and a common bounded support give convergence in L3.
For arbitrary real Fv​∈L3, choose such step functions Fv(n)​→Fv​ in L3. Assuming S=∅, refine their common atom levels, without changing the functions, to satisfy mn​≤minS−1. Apply the step-function estimate to these inputs. Lemma 5.2, summed over the fixed finite set S, gives convergence of their local integrals in ℓ1. The inequality ∣∣a∣−∣b∣∣≤∣a−b∣ permits passage to the absolute sum in (1.3), and norm convergence handles its right-hand side. This proves the theorem and its stated extension to real L3 inputs. The case S=∅ remains immediate.
For any coefficients ∣ϵI​∣≤1, the triangle inequality gives the corresponding bound for
k∈S∑​I∈Ak​∑​ϵI​LI​(F0​,F1​,F2​).
∎
